title: What we have handled (1 John 1:1–4)
hook: the word of life that we have seen and touched

segments.voice: Yesterday, a thousand years as a day, and a God with a very long fuse. Your line was he is patient. Who got an extra breath from you? Day six hundred thirteen.

You can read everything about the ocean. Tides, salt, the color of deep water. You can watch it in videos for hours. And then one day you stand at the edge and a cold wave runs over your feet, and the water teaches what the books couldn't. Hearing about it, seeing it, touching it: three different kinds of knowing. The first letter of John doesn't open with a greeting or a name. It opens with a witness, an old man, as tradition pictures him, saying: I'm not passing on a rumor. I was there. I touched him.
screen: `READING ABOUT THE OCEAN.` → `A COLD WAVE OVER YOUR FEET.` → `I WAS THERE. I TOUCHED HIM.`

segments.voice: Listen to how the sentence moves, in the Douay-Rheims: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the word of life." It starts out at the very start of everything, from the beginning, an echo of the opening of John's Gospel. Then it comes closer, step by step. Heard: you can hear someone across a room. Seen: now he's in view. Looked upon: a long, steady gaze. And handled: hands on. The Word that was with God from the beginning is something a fisherman could put his hand on. Why insist on this? Some scholars think the letter was answering people who said Jesus only seemed to have a body, that God would never really take on flesh, get tired, bleed. John won't have it. Later in the letter he says that every spirit which confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is of God. The Greek word for handled is the same one the risen Jesus uses in Luke's Gospel, when the frightened disciples think he's a spirit: handle, and see. And notice why John writes. So that you may have fellowship with us, he says, and our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son. The Greek is koinonia, which comes into Catholic language as communion. And so that our joy may be full. For Catholics this touchable faith runs all through the sacraments: water on a forehead, oil on hands, bread placed on a tongue or in a palm. God, in this tradition, keeps coming close enough to touch.
screen: `FROM THE BEGINNING, THEN CLOSER.` · `HEARD, SEEN, LOOKED UPON, HANDLED.` · `NOT A GHOST: COME IN THE FLESH.` · `KOINONIA: FELLOWSHIP, COMMUNION.` · then, large: `OUR HANDS HAVE HANDLED THE WORD OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch something as a reminder. Find an object near you that you can hold: a cross, a rosary, a mug, a smooth stone, or just the palm of your own hand. Hold it and breathe. Feel its weight, its temperature, its edges. Don't think about it, just feel it. Then let it stand for something: for this faith that says God came close enough to touch. If you pray, you can hold the object as a prayer without words. If you don't, just stay with the plain fact of touch, and notice what your hands know. The bell holds the time.
What we have handled. First John one: the word of life, heard, seen, looked upon and touched. Today's word.
Your line: seen and touched. Today, keep that object in your pocket or on your desk, and when your hand finds it, remember. Day six hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Catholic sacraments are celebrated with things that can be seen and touched, water, oil, bread, wine and the laying on of hands, and Catholics may keep a rosary, cross or medal close as a physical reminder of their faith.

original.note: Greek: (our hands) have handled (1 John 1:1). from psēlaphaō, to touch, to feel.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poetic way to say the apostles knew Jesus.
what it means: the Word that was from the beginning came close enough to hear, see and touch, and that's the root of the fellowship John offers.
what a scholar hears: psēlaphaō, the verb of the risen Christ in Luke 24:39, 'handle, and see'; some scholars think the letter answers those who denied his real flesh.

sources.quoted: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the word of life

notes: Tradition identifies the writer with John the apostle, an old man at Ephesus; the script says 'as tradition pictures him'. Authorship is discussed by scholars. Confirm framing.
'Some scholars think the letter was answering people who said Jesus only seemed to have a body' (proto-Docetism) is a common scholarly view, not certain. Confirm.
Psēlaphaō in 1 John 1:1 and Luke 24:39: confirm.
Koinonia → communion: confirm phrasing. 1 John 1:3–4 and 4:2 are paraphrased.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'from the beginning' (1 John) was called 'the same words that open John's Gospel' ('in the beginning'); now 'an echo'; Luke 24:39 brought to the Douay-Rheims wording ('handle, and see'; the disciples supposed they saw 'a spirit'); 1 John 4:2 paraphrase fixed to 'every spirit which confesses'; 'scholars think' softened to 'some scholars'; hook and practice no longer tell the listener what they know.
